A man in his 50s presented with new and progressive satellite lesions while undergoing pembrolizumab therapy. Two years earlier, he had undergone a wide local excision with graft repair for a left posterior auricular scalp lesion. On close inspection, milia and a few erosions with partially detached epidermis were identified. There were no abnormalities of the mucous membranes, nails, hair, or teeth. No extracutaneous involvement was observed.

Multiple pruritic erythematous to violaceous lichenified papules and plaques on the left shin. Close-up examination revealed erosion with partially detached epidermis and multiple milia.

vignette:
A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. Dichorionicity had been confirmed on first-trimester ultrasound. Pregnancy complications included early-onset growth restriction in twin 2 and new-onset preeclampsia at 30 weeks. At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed twin 1 with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid; twin 2 had estimated fetal weight <5th percentile, anhydramnios, and an absent bladder. Confirmatory ultrasound at 19 weeks revealed Tetralogy of Fallot in twin 2. By 21 weeks, twin 2’s amniotic fluid improved from anhydramnios to oligohydramnios (maximum vertical pocket 1.9 cm), and later normalized in both twins. Invasive testing was declined initially; at 31 weeks, chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 showed a normal chromosomal microarray.  
At 32 weeks, ultrasound at the tertiary center demonstrated:  
• Twin 1: estimated fetal weight 1904 g (62nd centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) 26 cm/s (0.56 multiples of the mean).  
• Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of vague, colicky epigastric pain radiating to the interscapular region, associated with anorexia and malaise. The pain was relieved by changes in sitting position and worsened by eating. There was no history of alcohol use, abdominal trauma, or pancreatitis. Routine laboratory studies showed thrombocytosis (platelet count >1 000 000/µL) and elevated blood urea. Aspirin (80 mg daily) was initiated for presumed essential thrombocytosis. 

An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a cystic lesion in the head of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a well-circumscribed, 11.8 cm cystic mass in the pancreatic head, without invasion of adjacent organs or lymphadenopathy. The serum CA 19-9 level was within the normal range. 

On physical examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation but no rebound or rigidity. There were no signs of portal hypertension or history of prior abdominal surgery.

vignette:
A 75-year-old woman, previously well, transferred her care to a new general practitioner in June 2022. She reported a presumed stroke in April 2020 with slurred speech, imbalance, and confusion lasting 48 hours; at that time, brain MRI showed chronic periventricular white matter changes without acute ischemic lesions, and CT angiography demonstrated carotid tortuosity with stenosis from myointimal plaques. Her medications included barnidipine 20 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

Since 2020, she experienced recurrent dizzying attacks characterized by sudden subjective vertigo, absence of nausea or vomiting, and unsteadiness with a wide-based gait requiring support; episodes lasted days to weeks and gradually resolved. Symptomatic treatments for dizziness were ineffective. Over months, attacks increased in frequency and duration until dizziness became constant, leading to loss of autonomy.

At the first visit, general and neurologic examinations were normal, and she reported a low mood. Days later, a severe attack prevented her from getting out of bed, prompting a home visit. Vital signs were normal; she was alert, oriented, and cooperative with normal speech. She described severe dizziness worsened by any movement or position change, without nausea or vomiting. With assistance, she sat on the bed with difficulty maintaining trunk control. When upright, she adopted a wide-based stance, was unsteady, and required external supports to walk. Romberg’s test was positive, with marked unsteadiness on eye closure. Strength and sensation were intact, reflexes were normal, and cranial nerves were intact. The finger–nose test was weakly positive on the right. The HINTS examination was negative.

A diagnostic algorithm for dizziness suggested a low probability of central or peripheral vestibular origin. Review of the CTA suggested that carotid stenosis had been overestimated due to marked vessel tortuosity. Transcranial Doppler confirmed tortuosity and plaques but demonstrated normal hemodynamics of the cerebro-afferent vessels. Repeat brain MRI showed no signs of recent vascular lesions.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

vignette:
A 74-year-old man with a history of interstitial pneumonia presented with one month of right-sided chest pain that worsened with inspiration and severe sweating confined to his right arm and thoracic area, accompanied by a cold sensation. He denied abnormal sensation or muscle weakness. Six months earlier, chest CT had shown dense infiltrates in the ventral subpleural regions of the right upper and middle lobes; on admission these shadows had enlarged. Oral antibiotic therapy failed to improve the infiltrates, and he was admitted for further evaluation.

On examination, he was sweating profusely on the right arm and right thorax. Vital signs were blood pressure 150/78 mmHg, pulse 71/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. A pleural friction rub was heard over the right chest. The skin on the right arm, chest, and back was moister and cooler than the left. Thermography revealed decreased surface temperature over the right arm and right thorax corresponding to dermatomes C5–T12. Pupils were equal and reactive; eyelids were not droopy. Neurological examination showed no sensory deficits or abnormal reflexes.

He had no history of smoking, trauma, or asbestos exposure. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and varicose veins, treated with candesartan and ezetimibe. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9,000/μL and C-reactive protein of 1.14 mg/dL. Intravenous antibiotics were started on admission, but his symptoms, inflammatory markers, and imaging findings did not improve. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed macrophages 65.1%, lymphocytes 4.8%, neutrophils 29.9%, and eosinophils 0.2%, with no microorganisms or malignant cells. A transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy or specific inflammation.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

vignette:
A 41-year-old man presented with a long-standing history of left plantar heel pain. Over two and a half years, he underwent extensive physiotherapy for presumed plantar fasciitis and tight gastrocnemius muscles, treatment with anti-inflammatory and analgesic medications, and two separate surgical releases (endoscopic plantar fascia release and minimally invasive gastrocnemius release) with only temporary relief. On re-presentation, he reported recurrent heel pain upon return to work.

On examination, he walked with an antalgic gait. The gastrocnemius remained tight with a positive Silfverskiöld test, and there was non-specific tenderness over the plantar aspect of the calcaneus at the insertion of the plantar fascia. 

Weight-bearing dorsoplantar and lateral radiographs of the foot demonstrated normal bony relationships with no fractures, lesions, or signs of arthritis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot showed no thickening of the plantar fascia and no signal alteration in adjacent soft tissues or bone marrow. However, MRI revealed a pedunculated bony protrusion arising from the posterolateral plantar aspect of the calcaneus, measuring approximately 1.1 cm × 0.9 cm.

vignette:
An 82-year-old man presented with painless right testicular swelling of several weeks’ duration without systemic symptoms. His history included glaucoma, prostatic adenomectomy, and hernioplasty; medications were dorzolamide, lansoprazole, and dutasteride. Testicular ultrasound showed enlargement and inhomogeneity of the right testis and epididymis with ipsilateral hydrocele. After 10 days of amoxicillin–clavulanate for presumed orchiepididymitis, swelling persisted. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed testicular pathology and revealed new bilateral macronodular adrenal enlargement measuring 15×12 mm on the right and 27×18 mm on the left, with homogeneous attenuation; these nodules were absent on a CT scan 3 years earlier. An 18 FDG PET/CT showed intense uptake (SUVmax 25.5) in the right testis but no uptake in the adrenal glands. Laboratory evaluation revealed normal electrolytes, blood count, iron studies, protein electrophoresis, glucose, renal and liver function, thyroid profile, LDH, and β2-microglobulin. Serologies were negative for active HCV and EBV (positive for past EBV). Clinically, he had no asthenia, headaches, abdominal pain, striae, or “buffalo hump,” and his blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg without hypertensive peaks on 24-hour monitoring.

vignette:
An 8‐year‐old boy with no significant past medical history presented with a 30-minute history of generalized abdominal pain followed by a single episode of vomiting. During the event he developed diaphoresis, mucocutaneous paleness, dizziness, dysarthria, incoherent speech, and lack of eye contact, without loss of consciousness, abnormal movements, or sphincter relaxation. The episode lasted 10 minutes, after which he reported a frontal headache (5/10) and persistent nausea. Family denied toxin or medication exposure. He had a similar episode 18 months earlier, diagnosed as migraine. There was no personal or family history of epilepsy or neurological disorders. Developmental milestones were age‐appropriate, and he was performing well in school.

On admission, his vital signs were normal except for blood pressure above the 95th percentile for age. Neurologic examination revealed confusion and disorientation; he could not recognize his mother or speak but could follow visual commands. Motor and sensory examinations were normal. Approximately 20 minutes after arrival, his consciousness and orientation improved. Over the next hours he had three additional self‐limited vomiting episodes and ongoing headache, which improved after a single IV dose of diclofenac (1 mg/kg).

Complete blood count, serum chemistries, and electrolytes (including sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus) were all within normal limits. Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol was reported as normal for age.

A 30-year-old woman presented with 2 months of worsening dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, and a 20-kg weight loss over 5 months. She denied fever, bowel changes, and relevant medical or malignancy history and had a negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR test. Vital signs were normal except for mild tachycardia (119 bpm) and oxygen saturation of 93%. Examination revealed decreased right lung breath sounds and minimal ascites. Labs showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (92 mm/h), albumin 3.3 g/dL, AST 32 U/L, and CA-125 121 U/mL (reference <35). Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions, right infiltrate, and cardiomegaly from pericardial effusion. Noncontrast chest CT confirmed bilateral pleural and pericardial effusions, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and lytic lesions in the sternum, right humerus, and thoracic vertebrae. She was treated for pneumonia, and dyspnea improved. On hospital day 5, PET-CT showed FDG-avid thickening of bilateral adnexa suspicious for primary ovarian malignancy, hypermetabolic osteolytic lesions in bone, hypermetabolic lymph nodes, pericardium, and pleura, and non-FDG-avid omental and colonic wall thickening. On hospital day 7, gynecologic ultrasound showed normal-sized uterus and ovaries with no masses or cysts, in contrast to the PET-CT findings.

vignette:
A 52-year-old woman with a history of long-standing diplopia was evaluated in clinic for persistent vertical misalignment. In 2005, MRI of the orbits revealed an anomalous band in the right orbit, which was surgically excised without improvement in motility; her diplopia remained stable in primary gaze. On examination in 2023, she was orthotropic in primary position but had an elevation deficit of the right eye. MRI of the orbits with and without gadolinium was obtained. The globes were unremarkable with no measured proptosis. The retroocular fat, optic nerves and sheaths, optic chiasm, and brain parenchyma appeared normal. A right orbital linear soft-tissue lesion was noted medial to the medial rectus muscle, parallel to it, with enhancement and signal-intensity characteristics identical to those of extraocular muscle, and it was unchanged from the previous study.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

width_distractors.label: Orbital myositis
width_distractors.rationale: Chronic orbital myositis can present with a linear enhancing lesion parallel to an extraocular muscle, though typically with pain and inflammation; granularity matches a specific diagnosis.

width_distractors.label: Orbital schwannoma
width_distractors.rationale: A schwannoma can arise along orbital nerves and appear as a well-defined enhancing lesion, clinically plausible and similar in diagnostic specificity.

width_distractors.label: Orbital dermoid cyst
width_distractors.rationale: Dermoid cysts are congenital orbital masses that may be linear or tubular, though usually with fat signal; still a plausible complete alternative diagnosis.

width_distractors.label: Orbital lymphangioma
width_distractors.rationale: Orbital lymphangioma can present as a soft-tissue lesion with enhancement, and may be stable over years; granularity is comparable to the reference.
